## The idea

Many large models consist of **independent parts that share a few resources**. In a
multicommodity flow problem, each commodity has its own flow-conservation constraints,
but all commodities share the arc capacities. In cutting stock, each roll is cut on its
own, but together the rolls must meet the demand for every width. In vehicle routing,
each vehicle drives its own route, but every customer must be visited exactly once.

@dantzig1960 proposed a decomposition that matches this picture. A *coordinator* (the
**master problem**) never looks at the details of the parts. It only sees **proposals**
from each part (complete plans for that part) and chooses the best *mix* of them that
respects the shared constraints. To steer the parts, it announces **prices** on the shared
resources. Each part answers with its best plan at those prices (the **pricing
problem**), the coordinator updates its mix and its prices, and the loop repeats. Dantzig
and Wolfe read this as a model of decentralized planning in a firm.

The device of handling a huge set of variables implicitly, by "pricing" them only when
needed, was used just before by @fordfulkerson1958 for multicommodity flows, and soon
after by @gilmore1961 for cutting stock. Today it is known as **column generation**.

## The structure Dantzig–Wolfe exploits {#structure}

The constraint matrix has a **block-diagonal** part plus a few rows that touch every
block. These **linking constraints** (or complicating constraints) are the only thing
coupling the blocks:

$$
\min \sum_{k=1}^K c_k^\top x_k
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad
\sum_{k=1}^K D_k x_k \le d \;\;(\text{linking}),
\qquad
x_k \in X_k = \{x_k : B_k x_k \le b_k\} \;\; (k = 1, \dots, K).
$$

## The reformulation: every block as a mix of its extreme points

The key fact is the representation theorem for polyhedra of Minkowski and Weyl
[@minkowski1896; @weyl1935]. Every nonempty polyhedron $X_k$ is the convex hull of its
finitely many **extreme points** $P_k$ plus the cone generated by its finitely many
**extreme rays** $R_k$:

$$
x_k \in X_k
\iff
x_k = \sum_{p \in P_k} \lambda_{kp}\, p \;+\; \sum_{r \in R_k} \mu_{kr}\, r,
\qquad \sum_{p \in P_k} \lambda_{kp} = 1,\quad \lambda, \mu \ge 0 .
$$

Substituting this for every $x_k$ gives the **Dantzig–Wolfe master problem**, written in
the new variables $\lambda$ and $\mu$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\min_{\lambda,\,\mu \,\ge\, 0}\quad
& \sum_k \Big( \sum_{p \in P_k} (c_k^\top p)\,\lambda_{kp} + \sum_{r \in R_k} (c_k^\top r)\,\mu_{kr} \Big) \\
\text{s.t.}\quad
& \sum_k \Big( \sum_{p \in P_k} (D_k p)\,\lambda_{kp} + \sum_{r \in R_k} (D_k r)\,\mu_{kr} \Big) \le d
  && \text{(linking; duals } \pi \le 0) \\
& \sum_{p \in P_k} \lambda_{kp} = 1 \quad (k = 1, \dots, K)
  && \text{(convexity; duals } \sigma_k).
\end{aligned}
$$

The master is equivalent to the original LP, and it has **very few rows**: one per
linking constraint plus one convexity row per block. The price is an **enormous number of
columns**, one for every extreme point and every extreme ray of every block. Column
generation deals with that by never writing them all down.

## Column generation: the algorithm

Work with a **restricted master problem** (RMP) that contains only a few columns, and
repeat:

1. **Solve the RMP.** This gives a primal solution $\lambda$, duals $\pi$ for the linking
   constraints, and duals $\sigma_k$ for the convexity rows. Its value $z_{\text{RMP}}$ is
   an **upper bound** on the master's optimum (for a minimization), since the RMP uses
   only some of the columns.
2. **Price.** The reduced cost of the column for extreme point $p$ of block $k$ is
   $(c_k - D_k^\top \pi)^\top p - \sigma_k$. The most negative one in block $k$ is found by
   solving the **pricing problem**
   $$
   \min_{x_k \in X_k}\; (c_k - D_k^\top \pi)^\top x_k ,
   $$
   an optimization over block $k$ *alone*, with the linking constraints moved into the
   objective at prices $\pi$. If it is unbounded, it returns an extreme ray with negative
   reduced cost instead.
3. **Add or stop.** Add every column with negative reduced cost to the RMP and go back to
   step 1. If no block has one, the RMP solution is optimal for the full master, and so
   for the original problem.

Because each new column is an extreme point or ray, and there are finitely many, the
process ends after finitely many iterations [@dantzig1960].

**A lower bound in every iteration.** Write $\mathrm{rc}_k^\ast$ for the optimal reduced
cost of block $k$. When every $X_k$ is bounded,

$$
z_{\text{RMP}} + \sum_{k=1}^K \min\big(0,\, \mathrm{rc}_k^\ast\big) \;\le\; z^\ast \;\le\; z_{\text{RMP}} ,
$$

so column generation can be stopped as soon as the two bounds are close enough.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Why the lower bound holds (Lagrangian relaxation)
Relax the linking constraints with multipliers $-\pi \ge 0$. For any such $\pi$, the
**Lagrangian relaxation** [@geoffrion1974]
$$
L(\pi) \;=\; \pi^\top d + \sum_k \min_{x_k \in X_k} (c_k - D_k^\top \pi)^\top x_k
$$
is a lower bound on $z^\ast$: any feasible $x$ satisfies $\sum_k D_k x_k \le d$, and
$\pi \le 0$, so $-\pi^\top(\sum_k D_k x_k - d) \ge 0$ only adds a nonnegative term to the
objective of a relaxation. By LP duality on the RMP, $z_{\text{RMP}} = \pi^\top d + \sum_k
\sigma_k$. Subtracting,
$$
L(\pi) \;=\; z_{\text{RMP}} + \sum_k \Big(\min_{x_k \in X_k}(c_k - D_k^\top\pi)^\top x_k - \sigma_k\Big)
\;=\; z_{\text{RMP}} + \sum_k \mathrm{rc}_k^\ast .
$$
Once $\mathrm{rc}_k^\ast \ge 0$ for all $k$, the two bounds meet.
:::

## A worked example

To see the geometry, take a single block in two dimensions:

$$
\min\; -2x_1 - 3x_2
\quad\text{s.t.}\quad
x_1 + 2x_2 \le 8 \;\;(\text{linking}),
\qquad x \in X ,
$$

where $X$ is the pentagon with vertices
\(0\.0\, 0\.0\)\, \(5\.5\, 0\.0\)\, \(6\.3\, 2\.2\)\, \(3\.6\, 4\.7\)\, \(0\.8\, 3\.6\). With one block, the master chooses a convex
combination of vertices of $X$ that satisfies the linking constraint. Its feasible region
in $x$-space is $\mathrm{conv}(\text{columns so far}) \cap \{x_1 + 2x_2 \le 8\}$, which
grows as columns are added. We start the RMP with the single column $(0, 0)$.

Star: the vertex returned by pricing, which becomes the next column. The arrow points along $-(c - \pi a)$, the direction pricing pushes toward. In the last panel no vertex has negative reduced cost, so the RMP solution is optimal.](theory-and-mechanism_files/figure-html/fig-dw-iterations-output-1.png){#fig-dw-iterations width=1046 height=952}

| 1 | 1 | 0.000 | -21.300 | 0.000 | 0.000 | -21.300 | (3.6, 4.7) |
| 2 | 2 | -13.108 | -15.096 | -1.638 | 0.000 | -1.988 | (5.5, 0.0) |
| 3 | 3 | -14.433 | -15.492 | -1.373 | -3.447 | -1.059 | (6.3, 2.2) |

Three things to notice:

1. **The first price is zero.** With only the column $(0,0)$, the linking constraint is
   slack, so $\pi = 0$ and pricing simply returns the vertex that is best for the original
   objective, $(3.6, 4.7)$. It violates the linking constraint, and the master can only use
   part of it.
2. **Prices steer the blocks.** Once the linking constraint binds, $\pi < 0$ makes the
   linking resource "expensive", which tilts the pricing objective (the arrow) toward
   vertices that use less of it.
3. **The lower bound is not monotone.** It goes
   \-21\.30 → \-15\.10 → \-15\.49 → \-14\.94. The duals $\pi$ jump from
   iteration to iteration, and so does the Lagrangian bound. This instability of the
   duals is a well-known cause of slow convergence in column generation; see
   [Practical issues](#practical).

The final master solution \(5\.9\, 1\.1\) with value
\-14\.942 is the LP optimum of the original problem.

## Dantzig–Wolfe for integer programs

The reformulation becomes most powerful when the blocks contain **integer** variables,
$X_k = \{x_k \in \mathbb{Z}^{n_k} : B_k x_k \le b_k\}$. Then the master is built from the
extreme points of $\mathrm{conv}(X_k)$, which are integer points, and pricing becomes an
integer program over one block. Often this is a well-studied combinatorial problem: a
knapsack problem in cutting stock [@gilmore1961], or a shortest path with resource
constraints in routing with time windows [@desrosiers1984].

Solving the master's LP then gives the bound

$$
z_{\text{DW}} \;=\; \min\Big\{ \sum_k c_k^\top x_k \;:\; \sum_k D_k x_k \le d,\;\; x_k \in \mathrm{conv}(X_k) \Big\},
$$

which equals the **Lagrangian dual bound**. It is at least as strong as the LP
relaxation, and strictly stronger unless the block polyhedra already have integer
vertices, the "integrality property" [@geoffrion1974]. The convexification happens
inside each block, exactly where integrality is "easy". This is the same idea as
[convexifying a disjunction](../../integer-programming/disjunctive-programming/big-m-vs-hull.qmd),
applied block by block.

**Branch-and-price.** The master's LP solution is usually still fractional, so column
generation is embedded in branch-and-bound: new columns are priced at every node of the
tree. Desrosiers, Soumis and Desrochers did this for vehicle routing with time windows
[@desrosiers1984], and @barnhart1998 laid out the general method under the name
**branch-and-price**. Branching needs care. Branching directly on a master variable
$\lambda$ is hard to express in the pricing problem, so one usually branches on the
original variables $x$ or on other structures that pricing can respect [@barnhart1998].

## Practical issues {#practical}

- **Tailing-off.** Column generation often finds a near-optimal solution quickly and then
  spends many iterations proving optimality, with the duals oscillating as in the
  example. **Stabilization** keeps the duals near a good point, for example by penalizing
  moves away from it [@dumerle1999]. The survey of @lubbecke2005 reviews this and other
  techniques, with an emphasis on the dual point of view.
- **Early termination.** Thanks to the Lagrangian bound, one can stop when the gap
  between the bounds is small, which in branch-and-price is often enough to prune a node.
- **Initialization.** The first RMP must be feasible. In practice one adds artificial
  columns with a high cost (a big-M "Phase I") or a heuristic solution.
- **Degeneracy.** Master problems are often highly degenerate, with many dual optima for
  the same primal solution, which also slows convergence [@lubbecke2005].

## Relation to Benders decomposition and Lagrangian relaxation

- **Benders is Dantzig–Wolfe on the dual.** Take the LP dual of a problem with linking
  constraints. The dual variables of the linking rows appear in every block of the dual,
  so the dual has linking *variables*, the structure of
  [Benders decomposition](../benders-decomposition/theory-and-mechanism.qmd#the-structure-benders-exploits)
  (see the side-by-side figure above). Generating a **column** for the primal master is
  the same as generating a **cut** for the dual. One method's pricing problem is the
  other's subproblem.
- **Dantzig–Wolfe is the LP dual of the Lagrangian dual.** The master LP and the
  Lagrangian dual $\max_{\pi \le 0} L(\pi)$ have the same optimal value
  [@geoffrion1974]. Column generation solves the Lagrangian dual by building up an outer
  approximation of $L$ with one linear piece per column, which explains both the
  lower bound above and the oscillation of the duals.
- **Where the strength comes from differs.** Benders keeps the integer variables in the
  master, so its cuts only see the continuous relaxation; see the
  [limits of Benders cuts](../benders-decomposition/theory-and-mechanism.qmd#limits).
  Dantzig–Wolfe for integer programs convexifies inside each block, so its bound
  reflects integrality at the block level.
